more.summary: A new study finds that tropical areas often thought to be safe from the effects of climate change are actually experiencing significant changes in rainfall and extreme temperature events. The paper, "Shifting climate in Caribbean tropical forests: Long-term trends at La Selva (Costa Rica) and El Verde (Puerto Rico)," is published in PLOS Climate.

more.title: Chinese writing developed square forms gradually, shaped by language, tools and tradition, analysis suggests
more.summary: A new historical analysis challenges the received wisdom as to why Chinese characters developed their distinctive square shapes. The work, published in the International Journal of Arts and Technology, argues that their shape resulted from interacting linguistic, technological and cultural factors rather than a single cause.

more.title: UK storm surges have far-flung, global climate connections
more.summary: Where a storm surge strikes along a stretch of U.K. coastline is decided by global climate patterns in the Atlantic, Arctic and even further afield—according to new research led by Cambridge University.

more.title: Scientists reverse liver cell aging and cut Alzheimer’s-linked protein in half
more.summary: A surprising discovery suggests that rejuvenating the liver could help protect against Alzheimer’s disease and heart disease. USC researchers found that an experimental drug restored aging liver cells in rats, cutting levels of an Alzheimer’s-linked protein in half and bringing bad cholesterol down to youthful levels.

more.title: Happy 65 Years: NASA’s Johnson Space Center Then and Now
more.author: Sumer Loggins
more.summary: Sixty-five years ago, a bold vision took root in Houston: a NASA center dedicated to human spaceflight. Since its founding, NASA’s Johnson Space Center has helped lead the nation’s human spaceflight program, supporting missions from Project Mercury through Artemis. Today, Johnson serves as NASA’s Center of Excellence for Human Spaceflight, and its workforce is helping […]

more.title: Gas inside us could fight wound infections, moth study shows
more.summary: A gas naturally produced by our own bodies could one day help treat skin and wound infections, potentially offering a new approach alongside conventional antibiotics.

more.title: Stem cells in deep sleep may point to a secret reserve for lifelong blood renewal
more.summary: Researchers at the German Cancer Research Center (DKFZ) and the HI-STEM Stem Cell Institute have discovered a group of particularly long-lived blood stem cells in mice. These cells remain in a dormant state for an exceptionally long time while retaining their ability to generate new blood cells.

more.title: Telltale furrows: What the Baltic Sea seafloor reveals about bottom trawling
more.summary: To what extent does bottom trawling impact the seafloor of the Baltic Sea—and how quickly does it recover? Two new studies from the Leibniz Institute for Baltic Sea Research Warnemünde (IOW) show that the marks on the seafloor provide a much clearer picture of the actual impact than vessel position data alone.

more.title: Arctic plant roots may play key role in climate change
more.summary: A new review involving researchers at Umeå University has revealed the critical role that plant roots play in shaping how Arctic tundra ecosystems respond to climate change. The paper, recently published in Nature Reviews Earth & Environment, highlights how processes occurring beneath the soil surface could help scientists better understand how one of the fastest-changing ecosystems on Earth will influence the…

more.title: Plants may experience 'optical illusions' that affect their direction of growth
more.summary: A new study from Tel Aviv University reveals how plants, despite having neither a brain nor a nervous system, integrate light coming from multiple directions to determine where to grow. The researchers show how this process emerges from local sensing across the stem, without the need for centralized information processing.

more.title: Why large dogs age faster than small ones, and other October research highlights
more.author: Jennifer Ouellette
more.summary: Plus invisible tattoos, medieval skeleton gets an ID, trapping a single antimatter particle, and more.

more.title: European flounder can complete whole life cycle in freshwater
more.summary: Most flounders sampled in Lake Pulmanki in northern Finland had spent their entire lives in freshwater. The study provides the first evidence of the species living entirely in freshwater. The work is published in Evolution.

more.title: Exactly solvable model reveals how trapped light can create magnetic order in one-dimensional spin chains
more.summary: A research team wanted to better understand how the forces between particles inside a material change. They discovered that by confining one-dimensional classical spin chains inside a mirror box cavity with light, they could force these magnetic particles to organize and undergo a phase transition.

more.title: Are we overfertilizing our fields? Researchers challenge conventional soil testing
more.summary: A new study led by Dr. Shikma Zaarur of the Hebrew University of Jerusalem, in collaboration with Dr. Ran Erel of the Agricultural Research Organization–Volcani Institute, reveals that agricultural soils may contain a substantial unaccounted-for reservoir of potassium, an essential nutrient for plant growth, that is largely overlooked by conventional soil testing methods.

more.title: According to science, you may be more likely to gain respect and status by helping others
more.summary: Human intelligence is still a bit of an enigma. Researchers have some ideas about why advanced intelligence evolved in humans, but they have not come to a conclusive answer. One prominent idea is that intelligence serves a social function. In their new study, a group of researchers led by Jonathan Egeland reports additional evidence supporting this idea.

more.title: Most of our measures of a key cognitive process don't agree
more.author: John Timmer
more.summary: A big study with very little beyond negative results still gets published.

more.title: NASA’s Hubble Uncovers Case of Missing Oxygen in Nearby Dwarf Galaxies
more.summary: NASA’s Hubble studied 37 nearby dwarf galaxies and found that much of the oxygen they expected to see is missing.

more.title: China imports millions of donkey hides from Africa every year: New book traces the drivers and impact
more.summary: The demand for donkey hides has grown exponentially over the past 15 years, driven mainly by demand from China. Lauren Johnston is a specialist on China trade with Africa. She has spent several years looking into the donkey trade, and has just published a book, "China, Africa and the Market for Donkeys." She answers questions about what she found.

more.title: How political disagreement with our neighbors relates to whether we bother casting a ballot
more.summary: In the 2025 federal election, Canadians voted at the highest rate since 1993. Explanations for high or low turnout usually focus on the national election campaign, including how close the race was and what seemed to be at stake.
